claim: Single molecule imaging has shown that part of actin disassembles within a few seconds after incorporation into the dendritic filament network in lamellipodia.
source: Single molecule imaging has shown that part of actin disassembles within a few seconds after incorporation into the dendritic filament network in lamellipodia, suggestive of frequent destabilization near barbed ends.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work on single molecule imaging.

claim: Filament severing enhanced near barbed ends can explain the single molecule actin lifetime distribution if oligomer fragments reanneal to free ends with rate constants comparable to in vitro measurements.
source: We find that filament severing, enhanced near barbed ends, can explain the single molecule actin lifetime distribution, if oligomer fragments reanneal to free ends with rate constants comparable to in vitro measurements.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results presented in the manuscript, specifically comparing simulated and experimental speckle lifetime distributions.

claim: The mechanism of severing near barbed ends and annealing leads to actin networks consistent with measured filament, end, and branch concentrations.
source: The same mechanism leads to actin networks consistent with measured filament, end, and branch concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to experimental measurements from electron tomography studies.

claim: The mechanism of severing and annealing leads to structural remodeling with longer filaments away from the leading edge at the +/-35° orientation pattern.
source: These networks undergo structural remodeling, leading to longer filaments away from the leading edge, at the +/-35° orientation pattern.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing filament length distributions at different distances from the leading edge.

claim: Imaging of actin speckle lifetimes at sub-second resolution verifies frequent disassembly of newly-assembled actin.
source: Imaging of actin speckle lifetimes at sub-second resolution verifies frequent disassembly of newly-assembled actin.
evidence: This claim is supported by new experimental SiMS data presented in Figure 6A showing short actin speckle lifetimes.

claim: The force for lamellipodial protrusions is provided by a dendritic network of actin filaments.
source: The force for lamellipodial protrusions is provided by a dendritic network of actin filaments.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The dendritic network is driven by actin filament polymerization, branch generation by the Arp2/3 complex and regulation of filament elongation by capping protein.
source: This dynamic structure is driven by actin filament polymerization, branch generation by the Arp2/3 complex and regulation of filament elongation by capping protein (Pollard and Borisy, 2003; Watanabe, 2010; Blanchoin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex nucleates filament branches at an angle of approximately 70° from filaments that reach the leading edge.
source: Activated by nucleation promoting factors on the cell membrane, the Arp2/3 complex nucleates filament branches at an angle of approximately 70° from filaments that reach the leading edge.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The dendritic lamellipodia network structure has been quantified by electron tomograms near the leading edge, revealing the number of barbed ends, branches and filaments.
source: This dendritic lamellipodia network structure, evident in electron micrographs of keratocytes (Svitkina et al., 1997) has been quantified by more recent electron tomograms near the leading edge, revealing the number of barbed ends, branches and filaments (Vinzenz et al., 2012; Mueller et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to electron microscopy studies.

claim: The lamellipodial network has a characteristic pattern with filaments orientated primarily at ±35° with respect to the protrusion axis.
source: Its characteristic pattern with filaments orientated primarily at ±35° with respect to the protrusion axis (Maly and Borisy, 2002; Schaub et al., 2007; Mueller et al., 2017; Koseki et al., 2019) has been interpreted by two-dimensional dendritic network models (Schaus et al., 2007; Maly and Borisy, 2002; Weichsel and Schwarz, 2010; Atilgan et al., 2005; Holz and Vavylonis, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental and modeling citations.

claim: Single-Molecule Speckle (SiMS) microscopy of fluorescently labeled actin revealed that actin assembly into the dendritic network is transient and not limited to the leading edge.
source: Single-Molecule Speckle (SiMS) microscopy of fluorescently labeled actin revealed that actin assembly into the dendritic network is transient and not limited to the leading edge (Yamashiro et al., 2018; Watanabe and Mitchison, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to SiMS experimental studies.

claim: In SiMS experiments, speckle disappearances occur within a few seconds after speckle appearances, a time which is relatively short compared to the time required for actin treadmilling through the entire lamellipodium.
source: In the lamellipodium, speckle disappearances occur within a few seconds after speckle appearances, a time which is relatively short compared to the time required for actin treadmilling through the entire lamellipodium.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from SiMS experiments cited in the text.

claim: Miyoshi and Watanabe proposed the hypothesis of frequent filament severing near barbed ends, following by annealing of the oligomeric fragment.
source: Since filament treadmilling cannot explain these dynamics, Miyoshi and Watanabe proposed the hypothesis of frequent filament severing near barbed ends, following by annealing of the oligomeric fragment (Miyoshi and Watanabe, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior hypothesis.

claim: In vitro experiments show dissociation of filament fragments from ends of actin filaments in the presence of cofilin and co-factors.
source: Consistent with the frequent severing near ends and annealing hypothesis, in vitro experiments show dissociation of filament fragments from ends of actin filaments in vitro, in the presence of cofilin and co-factors (Wioland et al., 2017; Kueh et al., 2008; Shekhar and Carlier, 2017; Andrianantoandro and Pollard, 2006; McCullough et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to in vitro experimental studies.

claim: End-to-end annealing of actin filaments is well-established in vitro and in budding yeast.
source: End-to-end annealing of actin filaments is also well-established in vitro (Sept et al., 1999; Andrianantoandro et al., 2001; Popp et al., 2007) as well as in budding yeast (Okreglak and Drubin, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: An independent-particle Monte Carlo model based on actin SiMS data used to model FRAP of actin in lamellipodia provided better fits with local recycling of slowly diffusing actin back into the network throughout the lamellipodium.
source: Additionally, an independent-particle Monte Carlo model based on actin SiMS data used to model FRAP of actin in lamellipodia (Smith et al., 2013), as well as actin monomer photoactivation experiments (Vitriol et al., 2015), provided better fits with local recycling of slowly diffusing actin back into the network throughout the lamellipodium.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling and experimental studies.

claim: A large fraction of slowly diffusing oligomers were observed in fragments of keratocyte lamellipodia.
source: A large fraction of slowly diffusing oligomers were indeed observed in fragments of keratocyte lamellipodia (Raz-Ben Aroush et al., 2017); however, the model developed by these authors did not consider or require the presence of a local recycling mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: Electron micrographs show that while a dense branched brushwork of filaments is observed near the leading edge (approximately within 1 µm), further away from the leading edge (approximately 3–4 µm away), filaments are longer and appear more linear.
source: Distributed turnover through severing and annealing may relate to another puzzle of lamellipodia structure revealed in electron micrographs (Svitkina et al., 1997): while a dense branched brushwork of filaments is observed near the leading edge (approximately within 1 µm), further away from the leading edge (approximately 3–4 µm away), filaments are longer and appear more linear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to electron microscopy observations.

claim: The model includes polymerization, depolymerization, branching, capping, uncapping, severing, oligomer diffusion, annealing, and debranching.
source: To investigate the mechanisms behind network remodeling, we created a stochastic model with polymerization, depolymerization, branching, capping, uncapping, severing, oligomer diffusion, annealing, and debranching.
evidence: This describes the components of the computational model developed in this study.

claim: Approximately 16% and 30% of actin speckles that appeared near the leading edge disappeared within 0.5 and 1 s, respectively.
source: Approximately 16% and 30% of speckles disappeared within within 0.5 and 1 s, respectively (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by new experimental SiMS data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: The large amount of short speckle lifetimes strongly supports frequent disassembly of newly polymerized F-actin near the barbed end.
source: This large amount of short speckle lifetimes strongly supports frequent disassembly of newly polymerized F-actin near the barbed end.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data in Figure 6A.

claim: The disassembly rate of Dylight 550 actin SiMS in lamellipodia of XTC cells was decreased by the treatment of 5 µM cytochalasin D.
source: The disassembly rate of Dylight 550 actin SiMS in lamellipodia of XTC cells was decreased by the treatment of 5 µM cytochalasin D (CD).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Cytochalasin D treatment results provide further support for rapid disassembly of newly polymerized actin at barbed ends.
source: These results provide further support for rapid disassembly of newly polymerized actin at barbed ends (either through 'bursting' as proposed in Kueh et al., 2008 or enhanced severing).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cytochalasin D experimental results.

claim: The density of tropomyosin SiMS was substantially lower in lamellipodia than in lamella in XTC cells ~30 min after cell spreading.
source: In this early phase, the density of TPM SiMS was substantially lower in lamellipodia than in lamella (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental SiMS data of tropomyosin.

claim: Tropomyosin SiMS are scarce near the leading edge, suggesting that tropomyosin may not have a significant effect on actin turnover near the leading edge.
source: TPM SiMS are scarce near the leading edge, suggesting that TPM may not have a significant effect on actin turnover near the leading edge.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the tropomyosin SiMS observations.

claim: Tropomyosin SiMS dissociated much faster in the lamellipodia than in the lamella.
source: In lamellipodia of XTC cells 30 min after cell spreading, TPM SiMS dissociated much faster in the lamellipodia than in the lamella (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing tropomyosin dissociation rates.

claim: It is unlikely that tropomyosin stabilizes actin filaments near the tip of XTC lamellipodia under the observation conditions.
source: We thus conclude that at least under our observation conditions, it is unlikely that TPM stabilizes actin filaments near the tip of XTC lamellipodia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tropomyosin experimental observations.

claim: The hypothesis of frequent severing and annealing provides a mechanism for distributed turnover and structural remodeling of the actin network.
source: We showed that the hypothesis of frequent severing and annealing (Miyoshi and Watanabe, 2013) provides a mechanism for distributed turnover and structural remodeling of the actin network.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the modeling and experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model is consistent with SiMS of Arp2/3 complex and capping protein in XTC cells.
source: Additionally, our simulations are consistent with SiMS of Arp2/3 complex (Millius et al., 2012) and capping protein (Miyoshi et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2011) in XTC cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to prior SiMS measurements.

claim: The presence of slowly diffusing oligomers assumed in the model could be consistent with the presence of slowly diffusing capping proteins in XTC cell lamellipodia.
source: The presence of slowly diffusing oligomers assumed in the model could also be consistent with the presence of slowly diffusing capping proteins in XTC cell lamellipodia (Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative connection between the model and prior experimental observations.

claim: The effective severing rate in simulations was 0.17 µM s-1 and 0.32 µM s-1 for different XTC parameter sets, which are a few times smaller than the experimental estimate of 1.8 µM s-1 for Aip1-associated filament disruption.
source: For the enhanced end severing XTC case in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3, the effective severing rate was 0.17 µM s-1 and 0.32 µM s-1, respectively. These values are a few times smaller, yet not too far from the experimental estimate.
evidence: This claim is supported by calculation from simulation results and comparison to prior experimental estimates.

claim: Filament shortening in keratocytes treated with low doses of cytochalasin D could be due to reduced structural remodeling of the lamellipodium through severing/destabilization near barbed ends.
source: This filament shortening could be due to capping by CD, as suggested (Schaub et al., 2007), however it may also be related to reduced structural remodeling of the lamellipodium through severing/destabilization near barbed ends.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of prior experimental observations in light of the current model.

claim: The results are robust with respect to the annealing rate constant and oligomer diffusion coefficient, as long as annealing is not dominated by reannealing to the same filament, diffusion is fast enough such that severing contributes to speckle disappearance in SiMS, and annealing does not occur further than approximately 1µm from the severing location.
source: Our results are robust with respect to the annealing rate constant and oligomer diffusion coefficient, which is why we did not elaborate on the precise length dependence of oligomer diffusion and annealing rates. Specifically, the results are valid for a range of diffusion coefficients and annealing rate constants, as long as annealing is not dominated by reannealing to the same filament, diffusion is fast enough such that severing contributes to speckle disappearance in SiMS, and annealing does not occur further than approximately 1µm from the severing location.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the model behavior across parameter ranges.

claim: The simulations showed how severing and depolymerization regulate the length of the lamellipodial dendritic network.
source: Our simulations showed how severing and depolymerization regulate the length of the lamellipodial dendritic network (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), similar to earlier models that have been formulated at various levels of description (Edelstein-Keshet and Ermentrout, 2001; Mogilner and Edelstein-Keshet, 2002; Carlsson, 2007; Michalski and Carlsson, 2010; Ditlev et al., 2009; Berro et al., 2010; Michalski and Carlsson, 2011; Lewalle et al., 2014; Manhart et al., 2019), including use of explicit dendritic network (Schreiber et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results and comparison to prior modeling work.

claim: Annealing was implemented in prior lattice models and lead to a wider lamellipodium, similar to the findings in this work.
source: We also included annealing, a process previously studied using lattice models by Carlsson and Michalski (Carlsson, 2007; Michalski and Carlsson, 2010; Michalski and Carlsson, 2011). In their models, annealing was implemented as reappearance of lattice links and lead to a wider lamellipodium, similar to our findings.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to prior modeling work.

claim: The model by Huber et al., 2008 included diffusion of free actin monomers, filament nucleation along predefined ±35° orientations, permanent barbed end capping, binding of ADF/cofilin and tropomyosin to filaments, as well as ATP hydrolysis and Pi release.
source: The model included diffusion of free actin monomers, filament nucleation along predefined ±35° orientations to represent branching, permanent barbed end capping, binding of ADF/cofilin and tropomyosin to filaments, as well as ATP hydrolysis and Pi release.
evidence: This describes features of a prior model for comparison.

claim: In the model of Huber et al., 2008, two distinct network regions formed with short filaments close to the leading edge, followed by a region with longer filaments starting at about 2 µm further away.
source: With this model, two distinct network regions formed (termed the lamellipodium and lamella in that paper): a region with short filaments close to the leading edge, followed by a region with longer filaments starting at about 2 µm further away.
evidence: This describes results from a prior model for comparison.

claim: The annealing mechanism in Huber et al., 2008 involved the joining together of any pair of filaments at the same distance from the leading edge, without accounting of the dendritic network topology.
source: The annealing mechanism (i) of Huber et al., 2008 is different to what we described in our work: in their study it involved the joining together of any pair of filaments at the same distance from the leading edge, without accounting of the dendritic network topology.
evidence: This describes a difference between the current model and a prior model.

claim: An annealing mechanism as in Huber et al., 2008 would not contribute to actin speckle appearances and disappearances and is likely inconsistent with SiMS data.
source: An annealing mechanism as in Huber et al., 2008 would not contribute to actin speckle appearances and disappearances (that were not quantified in their paper) and is likely inconsistent with SiMS data.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of a prior model for SiMS data.

claim: Raz-Ben Aroush et al., 2017 found evidence for the presence of a large pool of short actin oligomers in keratocyte lamellipodial fragments.
source: In a study of actin dynamics that combined experiment and modeling, Raz-Ben Aroush et al., 2017 found evidence for the presence of a large pool of short actin oligomers in keratocyte lamellipodial fragments.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior experimental study.

claim: The oligomer diffusion coefficient was estimated to be about 5 µm2s-1 for oligomers with an average length of 13 subunits in keratocyte lamellipodial fragments.
source: Using FRAP on small regions, fluorescence correlation spectroscopy, and phalloidin labeling, the oligomer diffusion coefficient was estimated to be about 5 µm2s-1 for oligomers with an average length of 13 subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental measurements.

claim: The finding of oligomers and the proposed distributed F-actin turnover by Raz-Ben Aroush et al., 2017 is consistent with main assumptions of this work.
source: The finding of oligomers, as well as the proposed distributed F-actin turnover, is consistent with main assumptions of our work.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current work and prior experimental findings.

claim: The absence of local reassembly in the mechanism proposed by Raz-Ben Aroush et al., 2017 may not easily explain experimental observations of actin FRAP or photoactivation over large regions of other cell types.
source: However we note that the absence of local reassembly in the mechanism proposed by Raz-Ben Aroush et al., 2017 may not easily explain experimental observations of actin FRAP or photoactivation over large regions of other cell types (Smith et al., 2013; Vitriol et al., 2015; Yamashiro et al., 2018), or the filament length increase across the lamellipodium.
evidence: This is a critical comparison between a prior model and experimental data.

claim: The mechanism of severing and annealing modeled in this work could represent a general feature of actin dendritic networks, including yeast cells where short actin speckle lifetimes have been observed in actin patches of fission yeast.
source: The mechanism of severing and annealing modeled in this work could represent a general feature of actin dendritic networks, including yeast cells where short actin speckle lifetimes have been observed in actin patches of fission yeast (Lacy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the model to other systems, supported by citation to observations in yeast.

claim: The mechanism might provide an energetically efficient mechanism for network remodeling matching different mechanical requirements: close to the leading edge, short branched networks would provide rigidity to compressive stresses while longer filaments at the back might be better suited for extensional stresses through myosin motors.
source: It might provide an energetically efficient mechanism for network remodeling matching different mechanical requirements: close to the leading edge, short branched networks would provide rigidity to compressive stresses (resulting from actin polymerization against the membrane) while longer filaments at the back might be better suited for extensional stresses through myosin motors.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional implications of the mechanism.

claim: Planar branching along lamellipodial plane sharpens the filament orientation pattern.
source: Planar branching along lamellipodial plane sharpens the filament orientation pattern
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results comparing different branching geometries in Figure 2.

claim: When the critical angle becomes smaller than 70°, the favored pattern is filaments with orientations centered at ±35°.
source: When this critical angle becomes smaller than 70°, the favored pattern is filaments with orientations centered at ±35°: the filament population around 35° can generate daughter branches at -35° and vice versa; thus the population sustains itself even as individual filaments get capped.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model.

claim: Uniform branching in 3D led to low and weakly varying order parameter, unlike the sharp orientation pattern with distinct transitions observed in 2D.
source: Uniform branching led to low and weakly varying order parameter, unlike the sharp orientation pattern with distinct transitions observed in 2D.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results comparing 2D and 3D branching in Figure 2B.

claim: A quasi-2D simulation with branching allowed to occur within 10° off the lamellipodial plane restored the behavior observed in 2D.
source: By comparison, a quasi-2D simulation with branching allowed to occur within 10° off the lamellipodial plane (close to the maximum off-plane angles observed in electron microscopy [Vinzenz et al., 2012] [A. Narita, personal communication, March 2018]) restored the behavior observed in 2D.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results in Figure 2B and comparison to experimental observations.

claim: Allowing kinking lead to a high concentration of filaments along the top and bottom plane of the lamellipodium but did not significantly influence the orientation order parameter.
source: Allowing kinking lead to a high concentration of filaments along the top and bottom plane of the lamellipodium but did not however significantly influence the orientation order parameter (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results comparing cases with and without kinking.

claim: The ±35° pattern does occur within a broad range of relative network growth speeds with uniform 3D branching, however the peaks at ±35° are not very pronounced.
source: We thus conclude that the ±35° pattern does occur within a broad range of relative network growth speeds with uniform 3D branching, however the peaks at ±35° are not very pronounced.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results in Figure 2.

claim: Experimental evidence in electron tomograms shows filaments oriented primarily along the lamellipodial plane.
source: Considering the simulation results as well as experimental evidence in electron tomograms for filaments oriented primarily along the lamellipodial plane (Vinzenz et al., 2012), for the rest of the simulations we proceed with the quasi-2D case where filament branching occurs within 10° of the lamellipodial plane and relative network growth speeds result in a ±35° orientation pattern.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to electron tomography studies.

claim: The assumption of slow barbed end dynamics away from the leading edge is consistent with the slow intensity increase in the back of lamellipodium after FRAP of actin or after photoactivation of actin at the cell middle.
source: The assumption of slow barbed end dynamics away from the leading edge is consistent with the slow intensity increase in the back of lamellipodium after FRAP of actin (Smith et al., 2013) or after photoactivation of actin at the cell middle (Lai et al., 2008; Vitriol et al., 2015), as well as evidence that cofilin and twinfilin promote both barbed and pointed end depolymerization (Wioland et al., 2017; Johnston et al., 2015; Hakala et al., 2021; Shekhar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to multiple experimental observations.

claim: A steady state with a finite lamellipodium depth is reached in the simulation whenever the net rate of depolymerization balances the net rate of polymerization at the leading edge.
source: A steady state with a finite lamellipodium depth is reached in the simulation whenever the net rate of depolymerization balances the net rate of polymerization at the leading edge.
evidence: This describes a fundamental property of the model.

claim: The model is in agreement with SiMS measurements of capping protein lifetimes in XTC cells, which were used as input to the uncapping rate constant.
source: The model is also in agreement with SiMS measurements of capping protein lifetimes in XTC cells (Miyoshi et al., 2006), which were used as input to the uncapping rate constant.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to experimental measurements that informed model parameters.

claim: The presence of slowly diffusing oligomers assumed in the model could be consistent with the presence of slowly diffusing capping proteins in XTC cell lamellipodia.
source: The presence of slowly diffusing oligomers assumed in the model could also be consistent with the presence of slowly diffusing capping proteins in XTC cell lamellipodia (Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative connection between model assumptions and experimental observations.

claim: For the parameters of Figures 4–5, release of capped oligomers through end severing would not contribute significantly to capping protein SiMS lifetimes, since the corresponding rate is 4–8 times slower than uncapping.
source: For the parameters of Figures 4–5, release of capped oligomers through end severing would not contribute significantly to capping protein SiMS lifetimes, since the corresponding rate is 4–8 times slower than uncapping.
evidence: This is an inference about the relative contributions of different processes in the model.

claim: The frequency of Aip1-associated filament disruption was estimated to be 1.8 µM s-1 in XTC cells.
source: Assuming that appearance of Aip1 speckles corresponds to filament disruption, the frequency of Aip1-associated filament disruption was estimated to be 1.8 µM s-1 (Tsuji et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior experimental estimate.

claim: The simulated overall effective severing rate was 0.17 µM s-1 and 0.32 µM s-1 for different XTC parameter sets.
source: We calculated the simulated overall effective severing rate by counting the total number of uniform and enhanced end severing within 20 s in steady state within 5 µm from the leading edge (average of 5 simulations). For the enhanced end severing XTC case in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3, the effective severing rate was 0.17 µM s-1 and 0.32 µM s-1, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by calculation from simulation results.

claim: The difference between simulated and experimental severing rates could indicate an even higher enhanced end severing rate in cells as compared to Figure 5.
source: This difference could indicate an even higher enhanced end severing rate in cells as compared to Figure 5, as also suggested by the comparison of experimental and simulated short actin lifetimes in Figure 6A and B.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the implications of the difference between simulated and experimental rates.

claim: Prior measurements of the intensity pattern of phalloidin-stained actin filaments in keratocytes treated with low doses of CD indicates shorter filaments compared to the control case.
source: Prior measurements of the intensity pattern of phalloidin-stained actin filaments in keratocytes treated with low doses of CD indicates shorter filaments compared to the control case (Schaub et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior experimental observation.

claim: The average length of oligomers predicted by the model is 40–80 subunits (0.11–0.21 µm).
source: While there is no direct measurement of actin oligomer lengths in cells, we note that our prediction of average length of 40–80 subunits (0.11–0.21 µm, Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2) is smaller to 0.25 µm, the length of diffusing actin filaments estimated by FCS in the cortex of Hela cells (Gowrishankar et al., 2012) but larger than 13 subunits estimated by FRAP in keratocyte fragments (Raz-Ben Aroush et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by model predictions and comparison to experimental estimates in other systems.

claim: Most of the F-actin at the back of the lamellipodium has undergone severing and annealing.
source: Most of the F-actin at the back of the lamellipodium has undergone severing and annealing (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.F), similar to an earlier particle model for distributed turnover (Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results tracking the origin of F-actin.

claim: The optimized parameter sets with speckle dynamics similar to SiMS experiments matched another observation from SiMS: the distribution of actin speckle lifetimes was weakly dependent on location of appearance with respect to the leading edge.
source: The optimized parameter sets with speckle dynamics similar to SiMS experiments of Figures 4 and 5 also matched another observation from SiMS (Watanabe and Mitchison, 2002): the distribution of actin speckle lifetimes was weakly dependent on location of appearance with respect to the leading edge (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results and comparison to experimental observations.

claim: The simulations implement a mechanism of local oligomer rebinding, which is needed to match actin FRAP and photoactivation data.
source: The simulations of Figures 4 and 5 implement a mechanism of local oligomer rebinding, which is needed to match actin FRAP and photoactivation data (Smith and Liu, 2013; Vitriol et al., 2015): as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B and Figure 5—figure supplement 5B the distance travelled by oligomers before annealing is in the sub-µm range.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results and comparison to experimental data.

claim: Simulated actin SiMS for parameters with enhanced end severing resemble experimental images from Yamashiro et al., 2014 and Watanabe and Mitchison, 2002.
source: As a further check of consistency of our simulations with SiMS results, simulated actin SiMS for parameters with enhanced end severing of Figure 4 (keratocytes) and Figure 5 (XTC) do resemble experimental images from Yamashiro et al., 2014 and Watanabe and Mitchison, 2002 (Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual comparison of simulated and experimental SiMS videos.

claim: Events that might be limited by spatial and temporal resolution or interpreted as blinking in SiMS experiments correspond to a very small fraction of speckle appearances in the simulation.
source: We confirmed that events that might be limited by spatial and temporal resolution or interpreted as blinking in SiMS experiments correspond to a very small fraction of speckle appearances in the simulation.
evidence: This is a verification of model consistency with experimental limitations.

claim: An alternative mechanism with frequent barbed end destabilization can come close to matching the three main experimental test criteria.
source: To test such a mechanism, we implemented a model with stochastic transitions to rapid barbed end depolymerization (see Materials and methods, Video 5). To maintain the F-actin loss by such a disassembly process, a process of rapid regrowth must also be included. Using the insight gained from our parameter searches with severing and annealing, we can show that such a model can be tuned to come close to matching our three main experimental test criteria: agreement with SiMS data, an increase in filament length with distance from the leading edge, and broad F-actin concentration profile (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results of an alternative model.

claim: The alternative dynamic-instability-like mechanism would require additional controls or homeostatic mechanisms to balance disassembly and reassembly away from the leading edge.
source: While we cannot fully exclude such a dynamic-instability-like mechanism, we note that: (1) it would require additional controls or homeostatic mechanisms to balance disassembly and reassembly away from the leading edge (while maintenance of F-actin mass is ensured by a severing and annealing mechanism), (2) ATP hydrolysis associated with ATP-actin monomer polymerization would be energetically more costly, and (3) reassembly of rapidly diffusing monomers away from the leading edge to recover bursting would also be less consistent with FRAP or photoactivation experiments (Smith et al., 2013; Vitriol et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of the alternative mechanism based on theoretical considerations and comparison to experimental data.

claim: The peak at t=0 is a general feature of a barbed-end disassembly mechanism where newly polymerized monomers are the ones that disassemble at higher rates, being closer to the barbed end.
source: This is a general feature of a barbed-end disassembly mechanism where newly polymerized monomers are the ones that disassemble at higher rates, being closer to the barbed end.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation for the model behavior.

claim: The experimental SiMS lifetimes in Figures 3—5 used a temporal resolution of 1 s.
source: The experimental SiMS lifetimes in Figures 3—5 used a temporal resolution of 1 s (Watanabe and Mitchison, 2002; Yamashiro et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the temporal resolution of prior experimental data.

claim: SiMS of Dylight actin was repeated on XTC cells using the methods of Yamashiro et al., 2014, with a temporal resolution of 0.1 s.
source: To probe the kinetics at even shorter lifetimes, SiMS of Dylight actin was repeated on XTC cells using the methods of Yamashiro et al., 2014, with a temporal resolution of 0.1 s.
evidence: This describes new experimental methods used in this study.

claim: Actin speckles were measured that appeared within ~0.5 µm of the leading edge, which should represent polymerization of actin monomers rather than oligomer annealing.
source: We measured actin speckles appearing near the leading edge, which should represent polymerization of actin monomers rather than oligomer annealing.
evidence: This is an inference about what the measured speckles represent.

claim: The speckle distribution in simulations extended to short lifetimes, similar to the experiments, with the percentage of lifetimes within 0.5 s and 1 s being 3% and 7%, respectively.
